title: Snare drum
reference_instrument: wires on, VCSL's snare drum 'modern 3' (Snare4), one wires-on hit at velocity layer v5 (Versilian Community Sample Library, CC0), a drum the card was not tuned to; VCSL holds no second take, dynamic or neighbouring note of that stroke, so no measure has a ruler. Wires off, nothing: all 14 VCSL wires-off hits (HitNS, on two drums) fail the screen's signal-to-noise check. Beside both strokes, with no count, stays the recording the head tension was tuned to: the Salamander Drumkit snare, 14x6, wires on, overhead microphones (Alexander Holm, CC BY-SA 3.0); the kit copies its sizes, not its materials. The distribution holds one overhead-labelled sample set and does not say whether close-microphone signal is mixed into it, so a line balance measured on it may not be comparable to an overhead-only render
summary: A 14x6 snare from the kit's finite-difference solver, one stroke wires on and one wires off. Wires on, it is graded against a VCSL snare it was not tuned to, but that set holds no second take, dynamic or neighbouring note of the stroke, so nothing is counted; the grader's pitch, the strongest line near D3, is 164.7 Hz against that drum's 143.7. Wires off has no VCSL stroke that passes the screen. DRSKit 2.1 (DrumGizmo, CC BY 4.0), which grades the kit's toms and cymbals, does not grade this snare: one of its 29 wires-on hits passes the screen on the right overhead, and the grader reads the render 402 c below that hit's note, outside its 400 c. The figures below compare with the Salamander strokes the head tension was tuned to. Shell, hoop and rim don't move, and edge, hoop and shell loss are zero, so wires off the low modes ring too long. Both clips now have air wall loss. Wires off, the strongest line is 152.5 Hz against 151.2 real, which is the head tension tuned to that line and so no evidence; wires on, it is 201.8 Hz against 235.5 real. Its two PET heads, air modes to 8 kHz and hickory stick come from sourced cards. The wires are coils of steel music wire pressed into the resonant head, with their count, tension and preload declared. Wires on, the attack is a little too bright: 28.2 % of the first 250 ms lies above 1 kHz, against 21.4 % real. Wires off, the sound is far too dark: 0.0972 % against 1.14 % real.
physics_present: Batter and resonant heads: tensioned PET film with its own bending stiffness and Berger nonlinearity, from a sourced film card
Head film loss: a causal material law on every mode of each head, from a loss curve derived from a published measurement of thin PET film
The exterior radiation load of each head from a baked baffled table, and the viscous boundary layer of the air on both faces of each head
Air inside the drum: cavity modes to 8 kHz coupling both heads
Wall loss of that air: viscous and thermal boundary layers at the walls, with their square-root-of-frequency law (Pierce 1981, sec. 10-4)
A hickory stick from a sourced wood card, with a Hertz tip transversely isotropic about the grain
Snare wires: coils of steel music wire with the maker's coil dimensions and the wire's measured stiffness and loss, with each coil's thermoelastic, bending and air-drag loss
A viscoelastic Hertz contact between each coil turn and the resonant head's film, in the wires-on clip
An overhead point about 1 m away that hears the drum as one closed body at low frequencies, both heads and a rigid shell over a floor, and crosses over to the baffled path above that
physics_missing: Head edge, hoop, shell and mount loss: stated unknowns, entered as zero

The recording's strongest line wires on: 201.8 Hz in the first 250 ms against 235.5 real, and the batter's (1,1) sits at 200.23 Hz later against the recording's 235.12. Wires off, 152.5 Hz against 151.2 real is the tuned head tension, not evidence
Spectral balance: the gap is 5.83 dB wires on and 9.02 dB wires off, where two real strokes differ by 0.90 and 1.81. Wires on, 28.2 % of the first 250 ms lies above 1 kHz, against 21.4 % real

Decay: wires off the gap is 1.57 octaves, where two real strokes differ by 0.67, and 250 Hz takes 780 ms from peak to -20 dB against 200 ms real. Wires on the gap went from 0.26 to 1.23 octaves, where the strokes differ by 0.51, and it is 0.485 without the 125 Hz band

The closed body is heard, not felt: the observer is outside the loop, so each head's radiation load is still its own baffled table, with no shell diffraction and no exterior coupling between the heads
Strand-end supports: each strand is pinned at the end plates with no strand-end or cord damping
The wires' count, spacing, length, tension and preload are declared estimates, not sourced

Wire torsion loss is omitted, and the air drag is the linear law, so the wires' loss is a lower bound. No print found measures the torsional loss of music wire in the audio band. Kim and Johnson (2007) measured a shear-to-Young internal-friction ratio of 1.104 for SAE 1050 steel by resonant ultrasound; times the music wire's excess bending loss of 1.4e-4 (Heptonstall, Waller and Robertson, by ringdown) it gives a torsion loss of 1.546e-4, which on the coil's 24 % torsion share would shorten the coil's T60 at most from 53.83 to 49.35 s at 100 Hz and from 7.61 to 6.74 s at 1 kHz, inside 8-3000 Hz only; that derived value is not in the model. A torsion pendulum on hot-rolled AISI 1095 steel at 7-15 Hz (Visnapuu, Nash and Turner, U.S. Bureau of Mines RI 9068, 1987) gives a loss factor of 4.77e-4 at its lowest stress, 17 MPa: an upper bound for that steel, not a value for the wire
Grid convergence: the snare isn't yet converged in grid spacing
The snare is simulated alone, so it doesn't buzz when another drum is struck
On the preset and live routes the strands are plain strings fitted to a recording (96ccf8f1b), not physics
